Mission & Vision

Data-driven crop improvement and ag sustainability.

ARISE-Institute is a South Dakota State University research hub that turns field, sensor, and genetic data into understanding the G2P relationship, leading to better crop decisions — from the breeding program to the commercial farm.

RE·SIL·IENT

Holds up under stress

Built for real growing conditions: Biotic and Abiotic stress and broader adaptability.

IN·FORMED

Grounded in the full data

Decisions built on comprehensive genomic and phenomics data — not a shortcut summary of them.

SUS·TAIN·ABLE

Built for the long run

Sustainable Ag (plant, soil, and environment) and sustainable research cluster.

Vision

An AI-powered crop genomics and phenomics research center that helps connect G2P and improve selection and management decisions — open to researchers, seed companies, and producers worldwide.

Two equations behind the mission

Crop improvement runs on genetics; better management runs on limits.

Genetics · Aim 2

R = h²S

R response to selection · h² heritability · S selection differential

The breeder's equation: each generation's genetic gain depends on how heritable a trait is and how hard breeders select for it. ARISE's phenomics work raises h² by measuring traits more precisely — directly increasing genetic gain, generation over generation.

Management · Aim 3

Growth = f( min of N, P, K, water, light… )

Liebig's Law of the Minimum: a crop's growth is capped by whichever resource is scarcest, not the sum of all of them. ARISE's precision-management tools are built to find that one limiting factor, field by field, and fix it.

Three research aims

From measuring plants to breeding and managing them better.

Aim 1 — Scalable phenomics

AI that measures plant traits automatically — from whole-field patterns down to individual leaves and grains — far faster than scoring them by hand.

computer visionphenotyping

Aim 2 — AI-enabled breeding & functional genomics

Combining smartphone, drone, and microscope images with genetic data to help breeders pick better parent lines, faster.

genomic selectionGWAS

Aim 3 — Precision crop management & digital twins

Satellite-to-soil sensing that helps producers fine-tune water, nutrients, and soil health across the season.

G×E×Mdigital twins

Seven stages, field to impact

The research pipeline behind every ARISE project, from an open question to a usable product.

Discovery
01

Biological questions & challenges

Addresses the core measurement bottleneck in crop improvement.

  • How do crops adapt to heat and drought?
  • Which root, leaf, and canopy traits best predict resilience and grain quality?
  • Can better models predict performance in genotypes and environments never tested?
Integration
02

Engineering tools & platforms

Modular, low-cost tools built to extend across crops.

  • Field instrumentation: cameras, thermal and hyperspectral sensors, drones
  • Controlled-environment and root phenotyping (rhizotrons, imaging)
  • Leaf and grain analysis: microscopy, spectroscopy, composition
03

Multiscale phenotyping

Root to canopy to grain, across time and environments.

  • Canopy — drone and field imagery
  • Leaf — physiology
  • Root — architecture
  • Grain — quality
04

AI pipelines & data integration

Scalable, reproducible, and transparent AI methods.

  • Multimodal data processing and trait extraction
  • Machine-learning models for trait estimation and cross-environment transfer
  • Integration with genomic and environmental data
05

G2P analysis & discovery

From data to biological insight and better prediction.

  • Genotype × environment × phenotype analysis
  • Identifying the traits and mechanisms that matter
  • Better prediction for genotypes, sites, and seasons never tested
06

Secure data management & sharing

Durable, shared infrastructure for the research community.

  • A governed data-and-model commons across partner states
  • Secure, FAIR data with access control and provenance
  • Shared tools, workflows, and models for reuse
Real-world impact
07

Products & impact

Resilient cereals. Stronger communities. A more secure food future.

  • Improved wheat germplasm for heat and drought resilience
  • Open-source instruments and AI tools, trained workforce, cross-state collaboration

Every output feeds a commercialization cycle run with SDSU's Technology Transfer Office — one that loops back into new Discovery work rather than ending at publication.

Discovery → Technical Proof of Concept (TPOC) → Commercial Proof of Concept (CPOC) → Development → Life Cycle Management ↻ back to Discovery

Why now

The tools haven't kept pace with the problem.

Agriculture needs to produce more with fewer resources, but the tools that could help — computer vision, sensors, genetics — are scattered across different fields and disciplines. ARISE exists to bring them together.

  • Most traits are controlled by many genes working together, which makes it hard to connect genetics to real field performance.

  • Measuring traits by hand is slow, subjective, and doesn't scale to the size of modern breeding programs.

  • AI models trained on one field or season often don't hold up in the next.

  • Public breeding programs have access to far fewer AI tools than industrial-scale operations that can build their own.

Publications

Already in print, with more underway.

ARISE's work is already producing peer-reviewed results, built on WheatAI — the lab's image-to-trait platform.

Publications

Figure 1 · Smart Agricultural Technology · CC BY-NC-ND

High-throughput estimation of wheat tiller density using UAV-derived spectral-textural features and attention-based deep learning

2026

Kaushal, S., Maimaitijiang, M., Subedi, S., Thapa, S., Koupal, D.J., Singh, M., Kaur, K., Kumar, P., Sitaula, P.R., Billah, M.M., Sehgal, S.K. — Smart Agricultural Technology, art. 1025214.

Counting wheat tillers by hand across breeding plots is slow, yet tiller counts strongly shape eventual grain yield. The team flew multispectral drones over SDSU wheat trials and combined dozens of color and texture measurements from the imagery. An attention-based neural network predicted tiller counts with about 82% accuracy (R²=0.82, ~15% average error), beating simpler models. That turns a days-long field survey into a few-minute drone flight, helping breeders screen more lines faster.

Figure 5 · Frontiers in Plant Science · CC BY

Predicting wheat yield and grain quality with UAV multispectral imagery and deep learning

2026

Billah, M.M., Maimaitijiang, M., Kaushal, S., Millett, B., Khan, S.N., Halder, J., Kleinjan, J., Sehgal, S.K. — Frontiers in Plant Science, 17, art. 1812052.

Breeders need early estimates of wheat's grain yield, protein content, and test weight well before harvest. Researchers flew multispectral drones repeatedly over seven South Dakota fields in 2022 and compared several machine-learning and deep-learning models. A 3D convolutional neural network using multiple flight dates performed best, explaining up to 69% of the variation in test weight and roughly 65% in yield. Imagery from the booting stage was especially informative, showing drones can forecast both yield and quality traits in-season.

Figure 5 · Scientific Reports · CC BY-NC-ND

Wheat spike and spikelet detection and counting from high-resolution digital imagery using YOLO with Oriented Bounding Boxes

2026

Ghimire, H., Maimaitijiang, M., Thapa, S., Kaushal, S., Koupal, D.J., Billah, M.M., Poudel, K., Sehgal, S., Singh, M., Subedi, S., Sehgal, S.K. — Scientific Reports, 16, art. 27355.

Counting wheat spikes and the spikelets inside them by hand is tedious, even though these counts predict a field's eventual grain yield. The team built a huge labeled image library — over 48,000 spikes and 60,000 spikelets — and trained two recent YOLO detection models to find them using tightly rotated boxes. The best spike detector matched manual counts almost perfectly (95.8% precision, 0.99 correlation), and the spikelet detector reached 99% accuracy. This gives breeders a fast, camera-based way to track yield-building traits at a scale manual counting can't match.

Figure 1 · The Plant Phenome Journal · CC BY

Deep transfer learning for grain yield prediction using UAV-derived spectral and textural indices across temporal and spatial domains

2026

Kaushal, S., Billah, M.M., Halder, J., Maimaitijiang, M., Sehgal, S.K. — The Plant Phenome Journal, 9(1), e70085.

A yield-prediction model trained in one year or field often fails badly when applied somewhere new, limiting its real-world use. Researchers paired drone-based spectral and texture data with deep transfer learning, which lets a model retrain itself using just a slice of new data. Fine-tuning with only 20% of a new year's data lifted accuracy from a failing score to R²=0.83, and 40% of new-field data lifted cross-location accuracy to 0.29–0.69. This makes drone-based yield prediction far more reliable across years, fields, and growth stages.
